name: Slagwall Forge Apron & Spatter Rig
description:
Heavy split-leather apron in deep charcoal grey, reinforced with overlapping carbon-ceramic tiles across the chest and thigh panels. The tiles are matte black hexagons, slightly irregular — each forge worker's rig develops a unique spatter pattern over years of use, a de facto record of their career. Worn over standard work clothes with a matching shoulder-wrap bib.

Shoulder straps are adjustable with quick-release buckles rated for emergency strip-off in under two seconds. Chrome arm wearers typically remove the left strap entirely and run a single cross-chest configuration. Street-manufactured versions from the Crucible district use reclaimed industrial leather with visible brand marks from previous uses.
functionality: Rated to 1200°C radiant heat for short exposure. Carbon-ceramic tiles absorb and distribute spatter impact. Quick-release shoulder buckles allow emergency removal in under two seconds. Adjustable strap configuration accommodates chrome arm prosthetics. Lower apron hem has a reinforced kick-plate against rolling slag.
what_it_says: Your work leaves permanent marks on everything, including you.
story_hooks: A veteran forge worker's apron tile pattern is recognized by a stranger as matching the splash signature from a specific industrial 'accident' fifteen years ago — one that killed six people.
Counterfeit Slagwall aprons with substandard ceramic tiles are moving through the Tier 2 market; the tiles look identical but shatter under spatter instead of absorbing it.
A forge worker's apron was left behind when they disappeared — the spatter record on the tiles tells a story of the last job they worked, somewhere they shouldn't have been.

physical_description.visual_profile: Heavy-duty protective apron with industrial presence. Deep charcoal grey split-leather body dominated by matte black hexagonal carbon-ceramic tiles across chest and thighs. Asymmetrical wear patterns and impact marks create a lived-in, battle-tested aesthetic. Paired shoulder bib wraps the upper torso. Silhouette is broad-shouldered and imposing when worn—designed for thermal and impact protection in high-heat environments.
physical_description.fit: Relaxed, oversized cut to accommodate layering and movement. Hangs from shoulders with adjustable straps; ceramic tile panels sit flush against the body with slight flex. Length extends mid-thigh. Designed to be worn over standard workwear without restriction. Quick-release buckles allow one-handed emergency removal.
physical_description.primary_material: Split leather (charcoal grey), carbon-ceramic composite tiles. Street-salvage versions use reclaimed industrial leather with ghost impressions of prior manufacturer marks.
physical_description.texture: Leather is worn smooth in high-contact areas, rough and textured elsewhere. Hexagonal tiles are matte-finish ceramic with subtle surface irregularities from thermal stress and impact. Edges slightly beveled. Individual tiles show micro-fractures and discoloration from years of spatter accumulation.
physical_description.color_scheme: Deep charcoal grey leather body. Matte black hexagonal tiles. Burnished bronze or chrome buckle hardware. Organic rust-orange and white spatter stains accumulate across tiles over time, creating a unique signature pattern per wearer.
physical_description.closures: Quick-release buckles on shoulder straps rated for 2-second emergency removal. Secondary friction-fit adjustment points. Chrome arm wearers often remove left strap entirely.
distinctive_features: Overlapping hexagonal carbon-ceramic tiles on chest and thigh panels
Unique spatter-burn signature develops per wearer over career
Street versions: visible ghost logos and brand marks from reclaimed leather
Asymmetrical wear patterns indicating dominant hand and movement habits
Micro-fractures in tile matrix visible under close inspection
physical_description.tier_indicator: Tier 3-4 working class. GeneFit manufacture signals official sector affiliation. Street-salvage versions (Crucible district) indicate Tier 4-5 fringe industrial workers.
physical_description.cultural_context: Marks the wearer as a forge worker, smelter tech, or heavy industrial fabricator. Spatter patterns function as a de facto résumé—depth and distribution of marks indicate years of experience and specialization. Wearing a 'clean' rig signals either apprenticeship or recent equipment rotation. Modified single-strap configuration with chrome arm removal is common among augmented workers.
physical_description.condition_typical: Always battle-worn. Tiles show accumulated thermal discoloration, spatter marks, and minor fractures. Leather creased and darkened from sweat and heat exposure. Buckles tarnished or corroded. Visible repair patches on street-salvage versions. The more damage and spatter, the higher the wearer's status in forge culture.
